Customer Journey Modellera guided demo on pragmatiq · which channel, which message, what time
Standalone offline snapshot · All 2,000 synthetic customers, 200 interactive scored customer profiles, stored evaluation results and charts are embedded in this file. No server or internet required. Training and live neural-network inference cannot run in a plain HTML file; token masking, customer-map clustering and ad-hoc predictions are clearly illustrative browser-side approximations. Fitted model metrics and the dashboard's saved customer decisions are unchanged.
Unpacking the included data…
1

Events and fake data

A customer journey is a sequence of actions by the bank (an email, a push message, a phone call, an in-app banner) and reactions by the customer (opening, answering, visiting a page, applying). Define which events exist and what usually follows what, then generate a year of fake customers. Every fake customer gets hidden traits: a favourite channel, a favourite topic and the hours they are active. Later steps check whether the model finds them.

2

Prepare the data: encode, tokenize, split

The raw text files (one per customer, the format a bank's systems would export) become what the model reads in three steps. 1 Encode: every line is checked and turned into typed values: a timestamp in microseconds, the source, the event and its fields, with numbers recognised as numbers. 2 Tokenize: every field becomes a key token and a value token, the words of the model's language; time becomes features, not tokens. 3 Split: customers are divided into train (80%, the models learn from them) and test (20%, they are scored on them). Bad lines stop the run with the file and line number. Hover a field to see its tokens.

3

Pretrain: fill in the blanks

The model learns what normal behaviour looks like by reading every customer's tokens with some of them hidden and guessing them back, like a fill-in-the-blanks exercise. Nobody labels anything. There are three kinds of blank: single tokens, every value of one field for a customer, and whole events. A hidden free-text field (a subject, a message) is not guessed as a word: the model rebuilds its 64-number vector, and we show the known texts closest to it. While it trains you see, live, one customer of every batch: what was hidden and what the model guessed. Once trained, try it on any customer.

4

Use the foundation model: segments, lookalikes, missing data

This is what deliverable 1 is for. After pretraining the model is used as a reader: a customer's whole token sequence goes in, nothing is hidden, and 64 numbers come out, a summary of that customer (an embedding). Customers who behave alike should get similar numbers. The map squeezes the 64 numbers of every test customer into two, so you can see who ends up near whom. Three uses are built below: segments (groups of customers with similar summaries), lookalikes (the customers most like a given one) and filling in hidden or missing data.

5

Predict the next event

Filling in blanks is not yet a forecast. To predict what a customer does next, a small extra model learns from past moments: given the 64-number summary and the last event, which event came next? The pretrained model stays frozen. Asked again on its own answer, step after step, it gives the flow of the next three events shown on the dashboard.

6

Objectives: what counts as success

The question we answer is which channel, with which message, at what time. For every customer we will compare the channels below and, for each, every message and every hour tomorrow, against doing nothing. Success is measured three ways: click-through, did they react (pick up, open the email, open the notification); conversion, did a sale follow within the next 10 events; and engagement, how long they spent on marketing pages and emails.

7

Decision models and quality

Small, fast models learn from past contacts: after an action like this, sent at this hour, to a customer like this, what happened next? They compare each action with doing nothing, which gives the uplift of every channel, message and hour. They learn from the train customers only; everything is scored on the test customers and checked against the hidden truth.

8

9

Try raw events

Paste raw event lines, exactly as a bank system would export them, and watch every step the model takes: parse the text, turn it into tokens, compress the history into an embedding, and predict what comes next. Change a line and run it again.

Raw events one event per line

timestamp ⇥ source ⇥ event ⇥ key=value ⇥ … · optional first line profile ⇥ age=54 ⇥ plan=plus ⇥ … · the Tab key inserts a tab · source is one of transaction, app, trading, communication
Paste or load raw events, then run inference to see each processing stage.

Choices and options: the foundation model

What has to be decided before building deliverable 1 on the real book: how to build the embedding model, what exercise it learns from, how big, and how long it takes, on which GPU, for a million customers. Every option with its pros, cons and cost; the outlined one is what this demo did.

Choices and options: the next-event forecast

Two ways to predict what customers will do: forecast their journey and read the outcome off it, or predict each outcome directly from the customer summary. Each with its pros, cons and cost; the outlined ones are what this demo did.

Choices and options: next best action

Three decisions shape the next-best-action model: where the effect of an action is learned from, which learner, and how the objectives are combined. Attribution, which past contacts earned a sale, is deliverable 4. Each with its pros and cons; the outlined ones are what this demo did.

Multi-touch attribution: which contacts earned the sale

A sale usually follows several contacts: an email, a push message, a call. Which of them earned it, and how many sales would have happened anyway? A forecast of the chance of a sale, from the foundation model's summary of the customer at the start of a 30-day window plus the contacts during it, is asked again with each channel's contacts taken out. The drop is that channel's credit; the chance left with no contacts at all is what the customer would have done anyway (organic). On fake data we know which contact really started each sale's journey, so every method can be checked.

Choices and options: multi-touch attribution

Two decisions shape the attribution model: how each contact gets credit for a sale and how to know the credit is right. Each with its pros and cons; the outlined ones are what this demo did.

10

Roadmap: one year to production

Everything above runs end to end on fake data. What it cannot prove is value on real customers. That takes real event exports, a foundation model trained on them, an intermediate release that A/B tests today's propensity models with its features added, and forecasting models in production for multi-touch attribution. Seven work packages over four quarters, with a go / adjust / stop gate at the end of each.
